title: Tailored multifunctional passivation enables efficient and stable flexible perovskite solar cells

title: High‐Entropy Prussian Blue Analogues as Cathodes for High‐Performance Aqueous Al‐Ion Batteries
summary: Prussian blue analogues (PBAs) are promising cathodes for aqueous aluminum‐ion batteries (AAIBs) due to their 3D open frameworks, which potentially facilitate fast Al 3+ transportation. However, their practical applications are severely hindered by poor electronic conductivity, suboptimal Al 3+ diffusion kinetics, and structural degradation. This study proposes a high‐entropy Prussian blue analogue (HE‐HCF) cathode through synergistic incorporation of multiple transition metals (Mn, Fe, Ni, Cu, and Zn) to enhance aqueous Al 3+ storage. This approach alters the local coordination environment, inducing the reduction of [Fe(CN) 6 ] groups and thus enhancing their reactivity. Moreover, density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal improved electronic conductivity and decreased Al 3+ diffusion barrier. When coupled with a polyvinylidene fluoride‐coated Zn‐Al alloy (Zn‐Al(P)) anode, the assembled HE‐HCF//Zn‐Al(P) full cell delivers a high capacity of 110 mAh g −1 at 0.1 A g −1 and a high energy density of 163.8 Wh kg −1 . Additionally, the full cell achieves a long lifespan of 1600 cycles at 1.0 A g −1 , which is attributed to the low fluctuation of lattice parameters brought from strengthened metal‐cyanide bonds within HE‐HCF. This work provides new insights into the design of multivalent ion batteries employing high‐entropy engineering.

screen.tldr: High-entropy Prussian blue analogue cathodes improve aqueous Al-ion battery performance via altered local coordination, better conductivity, and lower Al3+ diffusion barriers.

title: Dual‐Inductive and Programmable Switching: A New Paradigm in Ionic Interface‐Controlled Perovskite Memory
summary: While halide perovskite (HP) memristors exhibit significant potential for artificial neural networks, their reliance on stochastic filamentary switching severely compromises operational stability. Here, we demonstrate a fully programmable, forming‐free HP memristor that overcomes this intrinsic stochasticity through precise ionic interface engineering. By employing 1,4‐butanediammonium iodide (BDAI 2 ) as an ion‐modulating layer, we construct a structurally rigid, cross‐linked interfacial network strongly anchored to the 3D HP surface, forming the grain boundaries‐modulated barrier switching. The robust ion‐blocking barrier fundamentally suppresses random filamentary growth. Resistive switching (RS) is instead governed by dynamic interfacial barrier modulation, driven by the asymmetric accumulation of mobile ions that electrostatically modulates charge injection. Crucially, this stable non‐filamentary mechanism enables highly reproducible, bidirectional dual‐inductive responses, and distinct non‐zero crossing behaviors. For the first time in an operational HP memristor, we successfully achieved these combined dynamic features. We precisely control programmable multi‐level states governed by compliance current and operation velocity. This defect‐engineered, interface‐driven approach establishes a highly reliable and dynamically controllable paradigm for advanced neuromorphic computing and analog memory architectures.

screen.tldr: Halide perovskite memristor with an ion-blocking interfacial layer suppresses filamentary switching, enabling stable, programmable non-filamentary resistive memory states.

title: Investigation of Perovskite Layer Formation Processes and Their Applications in Optical and Electronic Technologies
comment: Integrated Journal for Research in Arts and Humanities
summary: Perovskites, as one of the new materials in the field of materials science and nanotechnology, are rapidly attracting the attention of researchers, especially in renewable energy applications such as solar cells and sensors. Despite the many advantages of these materials, there are many challenges in the process of forming perovskite layers that have a direct impact on the quality and final performance of the products. This issue highlights the need for a detailed and in-depth physical investigation of the perovskite layer formation processes. This paper systematically reviews various deposition methods, including physical deposition, solution methods, and thermal methods. In this regard, the effect of variable parameters such as temperature, time, and type of precursor on the growth and properties of the layers is investigated. The research methodology includes experimental study along with structural and optical analyses of the produced layers. The results of this study show that optimizing the process conditions can lead to the production of high-quality perovskite films with optimal performance. Also, these studies can help to achieve a deeper understanding of the relationships between nanocrystalline structure and physical properties and provide strategies to improve the industrial applications of these materials. Overall, this study emphasizes the importance and necessity of developing new methods in the production of perovskite films and opens new horizons for future research in this area.
